p: Friday, October 8, at seven in the morning, the go or no-go meeting for One Chart took nine minutes.

Maria had built it to be short. One page on the screen in the big room on the second floor: the exit criteria everyone had signed in August, with a column for met or not met. Testing. Contract acceptance tests, 7.3 included. The Rawlins volume test, rerun. Downtime procedures, practiced on paper on every Wyoming unit the Saturday before, with the plug pulled. Training, ninety-six percent of Wyoming users through their courses and a proficiency check, and no login for anyone without one. She read each line out loud. Its owner said met and signed. Gail signed for Rawlins last, the way she'd asked to, and capped the pen like she was closing a med drawer.

Ochoa had sat along the wall the whole time. On the way out he stopped at her chair. Cutover starts at midnight a week from tonight. I'll be in your command center in Cheyenne all weekend, he said. As furniture.
The command center roster was the last page in her folder. She'd written it three times. Days, seven to seven: Maria Santos. Nights, seven to seven: Kiran Bhatt.

Kiran read it standing by the coffee urn. He'd been back for five weeks, home by five most days, and the analyst Marcus had been teaching now built medications beside him without asking him first. In September you texted me at nine at night and asked who my second was, Maria said. This is my answer. He read it again. Twelve hours. Twelve hours. Then you go home and you don't answer your phone. Same for me. Command center rule. He pinned it to the wall of his cubicle, beside the monitor, where he'd see it at seven.

Her phone buzzed on the way back to her office. Lucia. 8 days. Maria typed back the first date she'd ever set for it herself. Saturday the 23rd. I'll pick you up. The answer came before she reached her desk. That's a date.

Monday, October 11, Gail called with a problem nobody had put on a page. The Rawlins emergency department ran on traveling doctors, locums, who flew in for a week of nights and flew out. Twelve were on the schedule for the six weeks after go-live. Seven had never used Corvane, and none of them could come to Wyoming early for the eight-hour physician class.
Corvane's training lead had an answer ready. Give them a tip sheet and a login. They're doctors. They'll figure it out.
Gail had already decided what she wouldn't do. Nobody works my ED on somebody else's login. Not after September. So tell me how these doctors learn it.

Kiran's team cuts the physician course down to what an ED doctor does at night: the track board, orders, the sepsis pop-up, a transfer out, and signing a note. Ninety minutes, online, with test patients. Each locum takes it before flying in, then sits with a superuser for a twenty-minute proficiency check, five tasks done without help. No pass, no login. On each locum's first shift, a superuser stays at the elbow until midnight. The first one, a doctor from Tennessee, passes on her second try and says she wishes every hospital did it this way. Gail writes the plan on her whiteboard under one word. Doctors.

Tuesday, October 12, Corvane's go-live support plan came over. One Corvane trainer for every ten users on day shift, at all three hospitals, and a phone number for nights. Rawlins would have two trainers on days, and the phone after seven.

Maria had sized the plan from census numbers back in February. Rawlins averaged fourteen inpatients plus whoever was in the ED, and its nights had one doctor and three nurses. Nights are where my trouble lives, Gail said on the call. A phone number at three in the morning is the help desk with a nicer name.

Twenty minutes later an email came in from 4 West at Greeley, forwarded by the nurse manager. Brooke had been a sepsis alert superuser since the spring, and she was asking to go to Rawlins for the first two weeks. Nights, she'd written, if anybody needed nights.

By Thursday it's one page. Superusers on every unit, every shift, for two weeks, then tapering as the ticket numbers fall. Rawlins gets one at the elbow on each unit at night and a second in the ED. Each superuser has a vest, no patient assignment, and a way to log every question to the command center. Corvane's trainers fill in on days. And twelve Wyoming nurses, two from each shift at each hospital, spent the summer in train the trainer sessions, so the skill stays when the vests go home. Brooke gets nights on the Rawlins medical floor. She answers the schedule with one line. Good. Nights are when nobody's there.

Saturday, October 16, MedaLink went read-only at midnight, and for six hours the three Wyoming hospitals ran on paper while the conversion loaded. Corvane came up at 6:04 AM. Maria watched it from a conference room on the second floor of the Cheyenne hospital, with eight phones, two projectors, and a whiteboard ruled into columns.

By nine the phones were ringing in waves. A printer in Laramie wouldn't print labels. A Rawlins nurse couldn't find a patient who'd been admitted on paper at 3 AM. A Cheyenne doctor wanted his old order set. Every call was real, and every one sounded like the most important thing in the building.

Ochoa sat at the far end of the table with a coffee and no laptop. Twice he started to stand when the phones lit up. Twice he sat back down. The second time, the call was the Cheyenne hospital president, asking for him by name. Ochoa pointed down the table at Maria.
Late that morning, Corvane's project director asked what Maria wanted on the board for the noon huddle. His tool could report ninety-one measures.

Six lines on the whiteboard, each with a target, emailed to every unit at noon and at six. Open issues by severity, and the age of the oldest. Severity ones resolved within an hour. Tickets per 100 users at each hospital. First-contact resolution at the desk. And two clinical lines Maria adds herself: doses scanned, and outside transfer med lists that arrived complete. At the noon huddle the Rawlins line is the worst, and the oldest open issue is the Laramie printer. Both have owners by 12:10. At seven Kiran comes in with a sandwich, reads the board top to bottom, and writes his name under hers. Hotel, he says. She goes.
Kiran's night report on Sunday morning had forty-one lines. Line twenty-three said: Rawlins, 3:10 AM, sepsis pop-up, bed six, order set started 3:14, superuser at the elbow, Brooke.

Maria called her at noon. Brooke sounded like someone who'd slept four hours and didn't mind. The nurse went to click it away. She was busy. I put my hand next to the mouse and said read it all the way down. A pause. I didn't, once. The patient, a woman with a kidney infection, had antibiotics running by 3:40.

Monday, October 18, at 6:10 AM, a Rawlins man with twenty-six active medications went to Greeley by ambulance. Nothing was faxed, and nothing went through Tributary. Nothing had to. The Greeley nurse opened the same chart the Rawlins nurse had closed, with all twenty-six in it and the last dose of each. Maria read the count off the command center screen and kept it to herself. There wasn't a page two. There wasn't a page. There was one chart.

At 9:30 a nurse from a hospital in Casper called the Rawlins ED. Casper wasn't part of Cascade. A Rawlins patient had gone there overnight for a heart catheterization, and the transfer document Casper always pulled from the regional HIE wasn't there. The newest one for any Rawlins patient was dated Friday. Marcus had the cause in fifteen minutes. The HIE had moved Rawlins to the new Corvane feed on Saturday as planned. Casper's system, and maybe others outside Cascade, still asked for documents at the old MedaLink address.

By noon the HIE has the list: nine outside organizations still asking at the old address. Two hospitals, five clinics, a home health agency, and the state immunization registry. Marcus and the HIE's engineer repoint them one by one, and Maria's team calls each organization to confirm that a test document arrives, then a real one. Until each partner confirms, Rawlins sends it summaries through the HIE's secure direct messaging, with a phone call to check the medication count. Casper confirms at 2:15. The Rawlins home health agency confirms Tuesday, and its director says nobody from Cascade has ever called her before about anything.

Tuesday, October 19, Renee called from Laramie at seven. Two of my surgeons are writing paper post-op orders again, she said. Pat's typing them in. Third day. The others are watching to see if it works.

Maria drove up 287 that morning and stopped at the door of the surgeons' lounge. Walt Hagen sat at the table in a lime green vest that said SUPERUSER, ASK ME across the back, with a clicker on a lanyard and a stack of order sets marked in red. He'd taken the train the trainer course in August, Renee said, and told nobody until he showed up in the vest.
He looked at her over his glasses. Don't say anything about the vest.
The two surgeons on paper had the same complaint. The post-op order set took thirty-four clicks, and paper took forty seconds. Walt had already counted. They're not wrong, he said. They're early.

Walt and Kiran's junior analyst spend Tuesday afternoon on the post-op set. The most common choices come up already checked, two screens become one, and it drops to twelve clicks. Walt tests it with his clicker and writes the number on the lounge whiteboard. Wednesday he rounds with the two surgeons, at the elbow, the way the vest says. By Friday one of them enters every order. The other enters most of them and complains about all of them, which Walt says is how you know it's working. Renee posts the unit's CPOE rate on the break room door every morning: 61 percent Tuesday, 88 Friday.
A text from Walt Hagen. CPOE 88. Post op set 12 clicks. A third surgeon asked for a vest. Told him to get his own. W.
It was the first text Walt had ever sent her. Renee said it might be the first he'd sent anyone.

Wednesday, October 20, at 2:15 AM, the Laramie pharmacy queue stopped receiving new orders. Kiran opened a severity one call with Corvane at 2:19, put pharmacy on its downtime procedure, phone and paper, and logged every minute. Corvane's line answered with a recording and an automated email. An engineer called back at 5:09.

Corvane's support agreement said a person would respond to a severity one call within thirty minutes, at any hour. Kiran's log said two hours and fifty minutes, and forty-two orders verified by phone in the meantime.

Thursday at eight, before Corvane's incident report came out, Brett Talbot called. You'll get our report at noon. I'd rather you heard this from me first. Our system starts and stops the clock on that automated email, so the monthly report is going to say we met the SLA. We didn't. Our night engineer for this region was covering two other go-lives, and nobody backed him up. That's on us. He stopped. My boss doesn't know I'm telling you how the clock works.

Maria answers Brett before anyone else. Thank you. I mean that. Then she does the rest in writing. Response is measured from Cascade's log, from the call to a person working the problem: 170 minutes against 30. The contract gives a service credit for a missed severity one, and Pam claims it. The November vendor review gets a standing line: response times by severity, measured by both sides, with any difference explained. Corvane adds a second night engineer for the region through December. Pam adds a line to the contract file: response means a person, not an email. Corvane's report arrives at noon and says met. Pam staples Kiran's log to it.
Friday, October 22, the end of the first week, Tasha sent the chart before the morning huddle.
Help desk tickets per day, first week of hypercare, all three hospitals. Tickets logged each day from Saturday, October 16, through Friday, October 22. Eight hundred twenty-four in all.

Under it she'd written what the chart couldn't show. For its size, Rawlins had by far the most tickets of the three hospitals, and the lowest share fixed on the first call. Most came from nights, and most of those said some version of the same thing: how do I move a patient to a swing bed.

Gail called after the huddle. My managers want to know if I should bring in agency nurses who already know Corvane, she said. Or send everybody back to class. Or wait it out. You've done this before. Tell me what to do.

Maria and Tasha bring her one page on Saturday morning. Rawlins: 180 tickets from 200 users, 90 per 100 users, against Cheyenne's 50. First-contact resolution 55 percent, because the desk couldn't answer swing bed questions any better than the nurses could. Three options. Agency nurses: expensive, and they'd know Corvane but not Rawlins. Class for everyone: twelve hours of nurses off the floor in the hardest week. Or a targeted fix: Kiran's analyst simplifies the swing bed screen, a superuser runs a ten-minute huddle on it at every night shift change, and the desk gets a swing bed script so it can answer on the first call. Maria recommends the third and says why. Gail reads to the bottom. The third one. And I'm keeping the page. A week later Rawlins is at 38 tickets per 100 users, and the desk fixes 81 percent of its calls on the first try.
Saturday, October 23, at seven in the evening, Kiran took the marker from her at the command center whiteboard. You have a date, he said. Go. I've got it.

She picked Lucia up outside her apartment in Greeley at 8:15. Lucia got in with her backpack still on, the way she had since kindergarten. Maria didn't drive to a restaurant. She drove to the hospital, up the parking garage ramp to the third level, and pulled into the spot by the stairwell. From there you could see the fourth floor. The ICU's lights were on, the way they always were, all night.
Is this where you parked? Fourteen years. Maria turned off the engine. In May she'd sat in Irene's driveway for six minutes before she could go in. This time she didn't wait.

So she told it. Her first year. A man sent down from a little hospital in Wyoming in the middle of the night, straight up to the ICU, no stop in the ER. A clot in his lung, and orders for a heparin drip. He was on high-flow oxygen and too short of breath to give anyone more than his name. Irene at the charge desk, pulling his medication list off the fax machine and putting it in Maria's hand. One page. It ended near the bottom, and it looked finished. There was a page two, Maria said. It never came through. His blood thinner was on it, warfarin. He took it every night with supper, and his doctor had raised the dose that week.

I had the heparin hung and the pump set. His baseline labs were drawn and not back yet, and the protocol let the bolus go first. I had it drawn up in my hand. Her right hand came up a little off the steering wheel, as if the syringe were still in it. The phone at the desk rang. Twenty to three in the morning. It was his daughter, calling from Wyoming. She couldn't sleep. She wanted to know if we knew her dad was on a blood thinner, because nobody had asked her.

I put the syringe down. I called the resident, and we got the lab to run his INR first. It came back at five point two. If I'd pushed that bolus, he could have bled into his brain, and nobody would have known why until somebody found page two.

Did he live? He lived. He went home eleven days later. His daughter drove him. I never met her. Maria looked up at the windows. That's the luck. Not me. A woman a hundred and fifty miles away who couldn't sleep. Nobody counted the pages. Nothing caught it. Somebody's daughter called.

I never told anybody. I thought it was mine. Then in May, at her kitchen table, Irene told me she'd handed me that fax without looking for a cover sheet, and she'd carried it all these years too. That page you found in her binder. Count the pages. She wrote it after. She called it ours.

Lucia had a lot of questions, and she started with the big one. Okay, but why not before? I asked you three times. Once for my essay. Once at the fridge with my matrix. Once over Irene's binder. You kept saying not tonight like that was an answer.

Because you're going to work up there, Maria said. Fourth floor, that desk. You'll be a new grad at that desk, and somebody's going to hand you a piece of paper at three in the morning. I didn't want you walking on with my story in your pocket, scared of every page. And I didn't want the first thing you knew about your mother as a nurse to be that she got lucky.

Lucia undid her seat belt so she could turn and look at her straight on, backpack and all. Mom, you put the syringe down. The phone rang. Yeah, and half my cohort would've told the daughter they'd call her back once the drip was running. Honestly I might have. You didn't do that. Maria put her right hand down in her lap. It was the hand that had held the syringe, and it had been up off the wheel since she started talking. Does it scare you? Knowing. Some. I'll count the pages. What was his name? I can't tell you. Privacy doesn't run out after eighteen years. I do still remember it.

Lucia's next question was a nurse's question more than a daughter's, and Maria liked her for it. So is page two fixed? For real patients, I mean, not in your test. Between our hospitals there's nothing to send anymore. The man from Rawlins on Monday, Greeley just opened his chart. And from outside? Casper, Denver, wherever. She had a point. Patients from other hospitals still came in through Tributary, one list at a time. How do you know those come in whole?
It's on my whiteboard. Every day. And when the whiteboard comes down? Maria didn't have an answer for that one yet.

Maria gets out her phone and writes it to Kiran while Lucia watches, because she'd rather do it tonight than mean to. Every transfer into a Cascade hospital from outside: the count the sender says it sent, the count that arrived, and whether reconciliation was done before the first dose. Weekly, by hospital, owned by the pharmacy director, who calls on every miss. Lucia reads over her shoulder. Send me the number too. So on Monday Maria does, and every Monday after. Outside transfers 37. Complete 37. Reconciled before first dose 35. Pharmacy calls about the two that day. Lucia answers each Monday's number with a thumbs up, and once, in November, with a photo of a plastic pill bottle from skills lab and two words. Counted it.

Tuesday, November 16, Aisha forwarded a question from Glenn with one of her own on top. Glenn wanted to know whether One Chart was costing nurses time. Aisha wanted to know whether she could tell the council it wasn't.
Kiran had pulled nursing documentation time per twelve-hour shift at Laramie from the system's own audit data: the median of MedaLink's last twelve weeks, then Corvane's first four.
Laramie nursing documentation minutes per 12-hour shift. The median of twelve weeks on MedaLink before go-live, then each of the first four weeks on Corvane.
Glenn's analyst had already done the math the simple way. Week one was twenty-nine minutes a shift worse than MedaLink, across three hundred nurses, and he'd underlined the total.

Maria sends them both the chart with the baseline median drawn across it. Four points, all above 142, all falling: 171, 163, 154, 148. It's a learning curve, it isn't over, and she says both things. Kiran adds Cheyenne, which is falling faster, and the Corvane hospitals from their own go-live years ago, which flattened near baseline by week ten. She asks for four more weeks before anyone calls it a cost or a win. With it goes the thirty-day survey. Nurses rate the system 3.1 out of 5, against MedaLink's 2.6 in the spring, and the top complaint is the swing bed screen, already fixed. Walt's comment says only: Discharge, 39 clicks. Measured. Aisha takes it to the council as written. Promising, she tells them, and catches Maria's eye. She learned that word from Maria in March.
Tuesday, December 7, Gail sent the portal numbers herself, with a subject line in capitals. CHRISTMAS CAME EARLY.

Since go-live, nurses and unit clerks had signed patients up before discharge, on the patient's phone or a caregiver's, the way they'd planned in July. Sixty-one percent of Rawlins inpatients had gone home with an account, against fourteen percent on MedaLink's portal. Gail wanted to tell her board.
Kiran had pulled one more number, and he sent it to Maria alone. Of the patients who'd signed up since October 16, twenty-two percent had logged in again after they got home.

Maria calls Gail with both numbers before Gail's board meets. Gail is unhappy for about a minute. Then she calls twelve patients herself. Most never got a notice when a result posted, because notices went to email by default, and half of Rawlins doesn't check email. Several live past the cattle guard and didn't know results could come by phone. Kiran's team switches the default to text, Rawlins nurses show each patient one result on their own phone before discharge, and the heart failure nurse in Cheyenne asks her patients to send one weight through the portal before their first follow-up call. By January forty-seven percent come back. Gail's board hears both numbers, and one more: nine heart failure patients sent weights in, and two got a medication change by phone instead of a trip to the ED.

Thursday, December 9, Corvane's quarterly upgrade was set for Saturday night, December 18, at every Cascade hospital, the first since Wyoming joined. The release notes ran 214 pages and listed 1,906 changes.

Kiran's junior analyst had read all 214 pages, which nobody had asked her to do, and flagged one line on page 141. The part of Corvane that read outside documents would now follow next-page links by a new default, set site by site. Corvane's note said no action was needed for most customers.
Corvane's upgrade lead wanted to keep the date. Seven hundred customers run this version already, he said. Test what you like. But if the eighteenth slips, it waits for March.

The upgrade goes into a copy of production on Monday. The junior analyst runs all 140 regression scripts, the edge scripts first: zero, nineteen, twenty, twenty-one, forty. The outside transfer script fails at twenty-one. The new default is set site by site, and Cascade's three newest sites came in with it switched off. Twenty of twenty-three arrive. She logs it as severity one, and Corvane fixes the setting in the package by Wednesday. Thursday she reruns everything, and it all passes. The upgrade goes in Saturday at ten, with every unit on its downtime view for ninety minutes, a back-out plan nobody needs, and a one-page note to every nurse about the three changes they'll see. Kiran forwards Maria the defect without a word. The subject line says page two.

Tuesday, January 4, at 7:30, the three-month benefits review was the only item on Ochoa's agenda. The plan the board approved in April set the first formal review at six months, but Glenn had asked for an early read, and Glenn didn't ask for things he didn't mean to use.

Each owner had sent a page. Gail and the other two CNOs sent scan compliance. The chief medical officers at Greeley and Fort Collins sent repeat workups on Wyoming transfers. The revenue cycle director sent denials, with a note that three months of claims weren't enough to say anything yet. Glenn's team sent the MedaLink invoices, the last one paid in November. Walt sent one line. 39.
Maria's draft summary had one sentence at the top. Rawlins scan compliance up from 62 percent to 95. It was true, and it was the sentence the board would remember.
Glenn had read it first, with his pencil.

Maria rewrites the top. Rawlins scan compliance was 82 percent before go-live: Kiran's eMAR pull for May through July, all shifts, the baseline the plan set once telepharmacy and the noon list had held, the same way he'd counted every dose for the restated report in February. December was 95. That's 13 points, and One Chart claims only that. The climb from 62 belongs to Cheyenne's night pharmacists and Gail's charge nurses, and the page names them. Laramie went from 81 to 94. MedaLink costs are gone on schedule. Repeat workups on Wyoming transfers are down, too soon to call. Denials: not yet. Each line is signed by its owner, Walt's included. Glenn reads to the bottom and sets down his pencil. I'll take this one to the committee as written.

The command center closed on Friday, November 12, four weeks after it opened. On its last morning Kiran erased the whiteboard except for one corner, where the junior analyst's name sat under his, and took a picture of it first. He sent the picture to Maria with no message. She knew what it meant: somebody else could take the nights now.

On the Sunday after she told Lucia, Maria had called Irene at noon, the way she did now. Well? All of it. The luck too. And? She said I put the syringe down. Irene was quiet for a second. Smart girl. Took you eighteen years to hear it.

Monday, January 3, at 7:02 AM, Maria sent Lucia the number, the way she had every Monday since October 25. It was New Year's week, so it was small. Outside transfers 9. Complete 9. Reconciled before first dose 9. Lucia answered in under a minute. Counted. Hospital clinicals start next week. Med surg in Greeley. They say I'll be at the elbow of a real nurse. Maria read it at a red light on Mulberry and laughed out loud, alone in the car.
Tuesday, after the benefits review, Ochoa kept her in his office. He waited until Glenn's footsteps were gone down the hall.
The board wants a three-year IT strategic plan at its March meeting, he said. I'd like you to write it, and present it.
That's the CIO's plan. It is. She waited for the rest. He turned his coffee cup a quarter turn, the way he did when he was deciding how much to say. Why does it have to be me?
Bring me a draft by February first. He opened his legal pad to a clean page. At the top he'd already written 2032, the year he'd written in July. Under it there was nothing at all.
